newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin orders disgruntled Lebed back to work.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin orders disgruntled Lebed back to work.

text.p: Alexander Lebed, Russia's outspoken national security chief, apparently threatened to resign on Thursday, forcing President Boris Yeltsin to play peacemaker among his squabbling entourage from his hospital room.
The 65-year-old president, appearing on television after meeting Lebed, said he told the general not to quit after he complained about Yeltsin stripping him of one of his many posts.

Yeltsin, who also made a radio broadcast on Thursday to say he was still in control despite preparing for heart surgery, told Lebed to get on with his job and work more closely with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Lebed had objected to the appointment of Yuri Baturin, his predecessor as national security adviser, to the chair of a committee on senior military appointments -- a post Lebed had held since joining the Kremlin staff in June.
"It seems to me Lebed does not have sufficient grounds for using this as a basis for saying 'In that case I should quit'," said Yeltsin, speaking slowly and directly to the camera.
"He (Lebed) needs to get down to business now, carry out the tasks he already has and make more effort to work with the premier and with the other services," added the president.
"You can't quarrel with everyone all the time. You can't settle issues that way. Our state apparatus must live in peace."
The president has been largely out of sight since before his re-election on July 3, prompting speculation that senior figures around him are jostling for power behind the scenes.
It was the first time Yeltsin had met Lebed since he appointed him his personal envoy to Chechnya on August 10.
In his radio address Yeltsin had given Lebed a special vote of confidence for his role in ending fighting in Chechnya. Lebed was jeered in parliament on Wednesday over his peace plan.
"My aide Alexander Ivanovich Lebed carried out my instruction and stopped the military conflict. The main thing is he succeeded in stopping the bloodshed," Yeltsin said.
Lebed, a 46-year-old reserve general who wants to be president, has had a lukewarm reception for his Chechen efforts from Chernomyrdin, a potential rival for Yeltsin's succession.
A third possible presidential contender, Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, took a new swipe at Lebed on Thursday, repeating his view that Lebed's Chechen peace deal was a "capitulation".

On Wednesday, Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais denied Lebed's accusations that Kremlin aides were manipulating the president and scheming against the security chief. Chubais mocked the ambitious general's generous appetite for publicity.
The chief-of-staff specifically cited Baturin's appointment as an example of how Kremlin aides let Yeltsin hear a variety of arguments but left the president to make a final decision.
Lebed and Chernomyrdin met Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev in Moscow on Thursday afternoon.
Yeltsin said he told Lebed the negotiations with Yandarbiyev had to be conducted "subtly and wisely".
In his radio address, Yeltsin warned that Lebed's peace deal left problems needing further negotiations with the rebels.
"It is too soon to stop worrying," Yeltsin said. "The separatists are approaching negotiations very reluctantly."
